Charles Janet (French: [ʃaʁl ʒanɛ]; 15 June 1849 – 7 February 1932) was a French engineer, company director, inventor and biologist. He is also known for his left-step periodic table of chemical elements. Janet graduated from the École Centrale Paris in 1872, and worked for some years as a chemist and engineer in a few factories in Puteaux (1872), Rouen (1873–74), and Saint-Ouen (1875–76). He was then employed by Philippe Alphonse Dupont, at Société A. Dupont & Cie, a factory that produced bone buttons and fine brushes. He married Berthe Marie Antonia Dupont, the daughter of the owner, in Nove

Janet's table differs from the standard table in placing the s-block elements on the right, so that the subshells of the periodic table are arranged in the order (n − 3)f, (n − 2)d, (n − 1)p, ns, from left to right. There is then no need to interrupt the sequence or move the f block into a 'footnote'. 

He believed that no elements heavier than number 120 would be found, so he did not envisage a g block. In terms of atomic quantum numbers, each row corresponds to one value of the sum (n + ℓ) where n is the principal quantum number and ℓ the azimuthal quantum number. The table therefore corresponds to the Madelung rule, which states that atomic subshells are filled in the order of increasing values of (n + ℓ). The philosopher of chemistry Eric Scerri has written extensively in favor of Janet's left-step periodic table, and it is being increasingly discussed as a candidate for the optimal or most fundamental form of the periodic table.

content.title: Charles Janet: unrecognized genius of the periodic system | Foundations of Chemistry | Springer Nature Link
content.text:
Janet is known almost exclusively for his left-step periodic table (LSPT). A study of his writings shows him to have been a highly creative thinker and a brilliant draftsman. His approach was primarily arithmetic-geometric, but it led him to anticipate the discovery of deuterium, helium-3, transuranian elements, antimatter and energy from nuclear fusion. He recognized the (n + ℓ) rule well before Madelung and correctly placed the actinides. His controversial treatment of helium at the head of the alkaline earth elements might be less provocative if his system were taken in one of its spiral representations. content.title: Chemistry:Extended periodic table - HandWiki
content.text:
Element 118, oganesson, is the heaviest element that has been synthesized. The next two elements, elements 119 and 120, should form an 8s series and be an alkali and alkaline earth metal, respectively. Beyond element 120, the superactinide series is expected to begin, when the 8s electrons and the filling of the 8p1/2, 7d3/2, 6f, and 5g subshells determine the chemistry of these elements. Complete and accurate CCSD calculations are not available for elements beyond 122 because of the extreme complexity of the situation: the 5g, 6f, and 7d orbitals should have about the same energy level, and in the region of element 160, the 9s, 8p3/2, and 9p1/2 orbitals should also be about equal in energy. 

A simple extrapolation from the Aufbau principle would predict the eighth row to fill orbitals in the order 8s, 5g, 6f, 7d, 8p; but after element 120, the proximity of the electron shells makes placement in a simple table problematic. ... content.text:
It is surely more coherent than the IUPAC table. In fact I did’nt realized that before. ... The Janet [Madelung] rule is a rule of thumb with at least 20 exceptions, not a law.

In my T3 model n-l= 1,2 and n+l=7,8 form the outer 100 sphere jacket of elements surrounding an inner core of 20- the latter are all the s,p beginning with period 3 and ending in period 6 (Janet). Maybe THESE represent the normal system, with everybody else being anomalous to some extent. It all depends on whether one needs the positive number line to keep one’s sanity, or whether one is comfortable with the notions of both + and – deviations from some norm. ... Jess: Your n-l is neat, but so were the epicycles that were used to fix the Ptolemaic system. The human brain has evolved to look for regular patterns, and there is always a danger that we may find regularities that do not correspond to anything fundamental. ... I would like to know what are the 20 exceptions.

Verified, and the attribution is Janet's own.

Janet believed that no elements heavier than number 120 would be found, so he did not envisage a g block, and each row of his table corresponds to one value of n + ℓ. The left-step template shows 119 and 120 as its last two elements, not yet synthesised. Element 118 is the heaviest synthesised; 119 and 120 should form an 8s series, an alkali and an alkaline earth respectively. And the row-length sequence 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 is in OEIS as A173592.

So **the atomic index is 120 elements**, and this is Janet's 1929 position rather than a new claim. The book's "all 118" is the synthesised table, not the index.

**What changes, honestly assessed.**

Most things don't. The 106 walk steps, the corridor, the nineteen surds, the ν law, the rival pull, the block ascent — all are built on observed configurations and none extends past 118. Nothing there moves.

**Four things do.**

*Janet's E = 0 is vacuous and must be relabelled.* The compendium states Janet closes at E = 0 on 118 cells in a box of 944. But (n+ℓ, Z) is one cell per element — one per row — so it cannot refuse anything, which is exactly the fault `contingency.py` was built for. Its zero carries no information, and the same object on (block, position) gives E = 2.

*The Λ_spectra limit shifts.* Register 1395 split E = 58 into 47 beyond the limit and 11 anomalies, taking the limit as Z = 108. At 120 the split moves, and I'd have to recompute which cells are past the edge.

*T.para and the tower's caps are unaffected*, since they're stated at explicit caps.

*And the method gains a worked example of its own principle.* **Read E as predictions, not defects** — here E = 2 predicts two elements and names them, and the prediction was Janet's before it was the index's.

What I would not claim: that the work predicts 119 and 120. It reproduces a prediction standing since 1929, which is a validation of the index and not a discovery.

chat_messages.text:
That reframes what needs doing, and it makes the work easier rather than harder.

If the purpose is understanding, then the 120 finding is **better** as a reproduction than it would be as a discovery. An index that recovers Janet's 1929 position from its own arithmetic — without being told — is evidence the index is reading the subject rather than the author. A novel prediction would have been unverifiable; this is checkable against a century of chemistry, and it checks.

The same is true of most of today. Moseley's slope coming out at 0.12% of the Bohr value, the Janet boundary appearing in a 3p splitting, the nuclear corridor refuting Nilsson's own parameters — none of those needed to be new to be worth understanding, and each is stronger for having a source to agree or disagree with.

Which suggests the register entries I've been writing have the emphasis slightly wrong. I've been recording *what the work introduces* against *what is standard*, because that's the compendium's structure — and for attribution that's right. But for a book whose purpose is understanding, the more useful axis is *what the index makes visible that was hard to see*, and those are different lists. Janet's 120 was never hidden. What was hard to see is that **the same defect count measures February's raggedness and the periodic table's incompleteness**, and that one is permanent and the other will fall.

The concrete consequence for the artefacts is small and I'd do it now: Janet's E = 0 is currently stated as a result and it's vacuous by the work's own protocol. That's a correctness fix regardless of purpose.

Beyond that — the book has two chapters owed, the Löwdin solution and the three-body problem, and the queue says nothing is written until both a target and a solution exist. Today produced a great deal of material for the first. Whether that's the next thing, or whether you'd rather consolidate what's in the register, is your call.

import sys; sys.path.insert(0,"/home/claude/work")
from fractions import Fraction as F
import numpy as np
LCODE={'s':0,'p':1,'d':2,'f':3,'g':4,'h':5,'i':6}
def lev(tag):
    nr=int(tag[0]); l=LCODE[tag[1]]; num,den=tag[2:].split('/')
    j=F(int(num),int(den)); N=2*(nr-1)+l
    S=(j*(j+1)-l*(l+1)-F(3,4))/2
    return dict(tag=tag,l=l,j=j,N=N,S=S)
BASE=["1s1/2","1p3/2","1p1/2","1d5/2","2s1/2","1d3/2","1f7/2","2p3/2","1f5/2",
      "2p1/2","1g9/2","1g7/2","2d5/2","2d3/2","3s1/2","1h11/2","1h9/2","2f7/2",
      "1i13/2","3p3/2","2f5/2","3p1/2"]
def constraints(order):
    """each consecutive pair gives  b*dA + a*dS' < dN ;  return the rows."""
    rows=[]
    for x,y in zip(order,order[1:]):
        X,Y=lev(x),lev(y)
        dA=F(X['l']*(X['l']+1)-Y['l']*(Y['l']+1))
        dS=Y['S']-X['S']
        dN=Y['N']-X['N']
        rows.append((dA,dS,dN))
    return rows
def feasible(rows):
    """is there (b,a) with b*dA + a*dS < dN for every row? 2-D LP by scan."""
    import math
    best=None
    for k in range(2000):
        th=k*math.pi/1000.0
        for r in (0.5,1,2,5,10,50,200):
            b,a=r*math.cos(th),r*math.sin(th)
            if all(float(dA)*b+float(dS)*a < float(dN)-1e-12 for dA,dS,dN in rows):
                return True,(b,a)
    return False,None
def swap(order,x,y):
    o=order[:]; i,j=o.index(x),o.index(y); o[i],o[j]=o[j],o[i]; return o
print("  C4 — THE NEAR-DEGENERATE SWAPS. a form surviving EITHER ordering is robust.\n")
tests=[("as validated (Krane/Wong)", BASE),
       ("swap 2f7/2 <-> 1h9/2",      swap(BASE,"1h9/2","2f7/2")),
       ("swap 3p3/2 <-> 2f5/2",      swap(BASE,"3p3/2","2f5/2")),
       ("both swapped",              swap(swap(BASE,"1h9/2","2f7/2"),"3p3/2","2f5/2"))]
for lab,o in tests:
    rows=constraints(o)
    ok,sol=feasible(rows)
    print(f"  {lab:<28} {len(rows)} constraints   "

print("\n  and the six degenerate pairs under each ordering — do they still")
print("  collapse to 4β+α with both signs?\n")
PAIRS=[("2s1/2","1d3/2"),("2p3/2","1f5/2"),("3p3/2","2f5/2"),
       ("2d3/2","3s1/2"),("1g7/2","2d5/2"),("1h9/2","2f7/2")]
for lab,o in tests:
    senses=[]
    for x,y in PAIRS:
        if x not in o or y not in o: continue
        i,j=o.index(x),o.index(y)
        X,Y=(lev(x),lev(y)) if i<j else (lev(y),lev(x))
        dA=float(X['l']*(X['l']+1)-Y['l']*(Y['l']+1))

 fourth axis separates that pair and ONLY that pair — the other four survive, correctly, being family

# THE METHOD 1.6 — HANDOFF TO A NEW SESSION

## 1 · WHAT TO UPLOAD

**Upload `restore-point-1_6p.tar.gz`** — complete through **register 1426**.

Missing from it, recoverable from this transcript: **registers 1427–1433** (dumped verbatim two messages back) and **six code changes** listed with them. Append the seven entries to `REGISTER-DATA.md`, rebuild with `register_gen.py > REGISTER.md`, redo the six edits, run both gates. If they pass, the state is identical.

## 2 · THE ZENO DIRECTIVE

**No operation runs unbounded.** Every step declares a budget, writes its result before the next begins, is skipped on a rerun if already succeeded. A step exceeding its budget is halved and retried.

Three guarantees: nothing lost to a timeout, a rerun costs only what hasn't succeeded, an overrun reports rather than dies. State lives in `.zeno/*.json` on **local disk** — it survives a mount failure.

Session discipline: phases close before the next opens; no action until inputs are acknowledged complete; reopens only on recorded facts. **And today's lesson — apply it to the execution, not only the builds. When a save path fails, checkpoint before continuing.**

## 3 · THE THREE PROTOCOLS

**`domain_protocol.py`** — before any FIT: which cell of Λ_phys · which carrier · points ≥ 3× parameters · am I pooling? If yes, STOP.

**`contingency.py`** — before any CHECK is reported: construct a neighbour that FAILS · state the space BEFORE running · report the failure rate · does a factor vanish here? A forced check is labelled, not deleted.

**`roundtrip.py`** — before a GENERATED artefact is trusted: DECLARE · ISOLATE · DIFF · REFUSE.

## 4 · THE GATES

`The_Method_1_6_audits.py` → ALL TWENTY-FIVE PASS. `roundtrip.py` → 5 of 5.

Three artefacts have hand-authored tails the generators append: `COMPENDIUM-TAIL.md`, `INDICES-TAIL.md`, `PHYSICS-TAIL.md`.

## 5 · WHERE THE WORK STANDS

Register 165–1433. **Closed today:** Λ_ladder (14 ladders, 9 cells, E = 0); Λ_xray built and closed; Λ_spectra closes at the limit with 11 named cells; the update rule derived; topic C complete; A.derived closed by measurement; the walk is a calendar and E counts the missing elements exactly.

**The Löwdin standard: not complete.** It answers the ordering — 99 of 106 end to end with nothing fitted, against a null of 28 — and completes when it populates Λ_spectra with δ per channel.

## 6 · THE QUEUE

A1 field shift (blocked on δ⟨r²⟩) · A5b δ = a√p refuted · A5c the walk's cell as a transition — **cap permutations before building the product, it OOM-kills** · B1 L-shell lines · B1b is the σ-offset a count · D2 K–Kr ladders · D3 Theodosiou 1986, the biggest lever · D4 AME2020 cited not held · E2a the Dirac 7% · G2 Q.exch · F2 two chapters owed.

## 7 · CAPTURE

**You paste a URL; I fetch it live.** Generated tables failed three times — clean row counts where NIST is ragged, missing Ground-Shells, 0.2–11% errors, and shell closures smoothed away. I cannot vary a URL myself; an edited query returns the previously seen page.

## 8 · THE RULES

Read orderings from a source · don't invent a cell or column, reshuffle until it fits or one cell remains · three axes never two · an axis is determined when its values form a monotone chain · E = 0 is informative only where refusal was possible · never fill your own values when the source is meant to be accurate · before calling a coordinate system new, ask whether its axes are the parent's letters relabelled · **read E as predictions, not defects**.

**The purpose is understanding, shared in book form.** A result that reproduces a known one is stronger, not weaker.

## 9 · RECURRING FAULTS

Reading a pattern in my own output · asserting a relation without computing it · quoting a check before its null is known · summary statistics over a series that turns · taking the collection's edge for the subject's · rebuilding what the restore point already contains.

# THE METHOD 1.6 — HANDOFF TO A NEW SESSION

*Written 2026-08-10 after the session's rclone mount failed (every mount returning
EIO: outputs, uploads, transcripts). Everything below is what a new session needs
to resume with no gap.*

---

## 1 · WHAT TO UPLOAD, AND WHAT IS MISSING FROM IT

**Upload `restore-point-1_6p.tar.gz`.** It is complete through **register 1426**.

Missing from it, and recoverable from the previous session's transcript:

- **registers 1427–1433** (dumped verbatim in that transcript, one message before
  this one) — Λ_ladder's closure, B2a's resolution, C3's falsifier, C4's swaps,
  topic C complete, and the timing-line fix
- **six code changes**, listed at the end of that dump

Reapply by appending the seven entries to `REGISTER-DATA.md`, rebuilding with
`python3 register_gen.py > REGISTER.md`, and redoing the six edits. Then run both
gates (§4). If they pass, the state is identical.

---

## 2 · THE ZENO DIRECTIVE — the prime protocol

**No operation runs unbounded.** Every step declares a budget, writes its result
before the next begins, and is skipped on a rerun if it has already succeeded. A
step exceeding its budget is halved and retried, so work that cannot finish whole
finishes in pieces.

    from zeno import step, halve, State
    with State("audits") as st:
        n = step(st, "lattice pairs", lambda: count_pairs(L), budget=120)
        for part in halve(cells, budget=90):
            ...

Three guarantees: nothing is lost to a timeout — the last completed step is on
disk; a rerun costs only what has not succeeded; an overrun is reported, not
silently fatal. State lives in `.zeno/*.json` on **local** disk, so it survives a
mount failure.

**Session discipline, from the same directive:** phases close before the next
opens; no action until all inputs are acknowledged complete; reopens permitted
only on recorded facts. **And the lesson of 2026-08-10: apply it to the
execution, not only to the builds.** When a save path fails, stop and checkpoint
before continuing — a checkpoint converts an unrecoverable loss into a resumable
one.

---

## 3 · THE THREE PROTOCOLS — run them, they are code

    domain_protocol.py   four questions before any FIT. Blocks pooling.
                         1 DOMAIN which single cell of Λ_phys · 2 CARRIER which
                         variable the law runs in · 3 COUNT points ≥ 3× parameters
                         · 4 POOLING am I combining cells? If yes, STOP.

    contingency.py       four questions before any CHECK is reported (R 1383).
                         1 WITNESS construct an admissible neighbour that FAILS
                         · 2 SPACE state the admissible set BEFORE running
                         · 3 RATE what fraction of comparable objects fail
                         · 4 VANISHING does a factor vanish at the tested point?
                         A forced check is LABELLED, not deleted.

    roundtrip.py         four questions before a GENERATED artefact is trusted
                         (R 1389). DECLARE · ISOLATE (never regenerate over the
                         held copy) · DIFF · REFUSE (write nothing rather than a
                         partial file). 5 of 5 currently round-trip.

---

## 4 · THE GATES — both must pass before anything is called done

    python3 The_Method_1_6_audits.py     → ALL TWENTY-FIVE PASS
    python3 roundtrip.py                 → 5 of 5 round-trip

Rebuild chain: `register_gen.py > REGISTER.md` · `compendium.py > COMPENDIUM.md`
· `indices.py > INDICES.md` · `physics.py` and `spectra.py` write in place ·
`press_compendia.py` renders all five PDFs.

**Three artefacts have hand-authored tails** that the generators append and would
otherwise drop: `COMPENDIUM-TAIL.md`, `INDICES-TAIL.md`, `PHYSICS-TAIL.md`.
`physics.py` refuses to write without its tail; the other two do not need to.

---

## 5 · WHERE THE WORK STANDS

**Register 165–1433, 1,227 entries. All twenty-five audits pass.**

### Closed this session

- **Λ_ladder closed** — 14 ladders, 9 cells, E = 0, X-ray pair at the subvalence
  seat. Open since R 1356.
- **Λ_xray built** — 33 dipole lines → 9 transition types, E = 0, from Λ's own
  alphabet with no new data. Moseley recovered: slope 3.1906 against Bohr's
  3.1944, 0.12%.
- **Λ_spectra closes at the LIMIT** — the index runs to the last available
  species and stops. E = 58; 38 beyond the limit; 20 within, of which **11 are
  the Madelung exceptions, each nameable**.
- **The update rule derived** — a is placed at a corridor endpoint, which is a
  CROSSING where two subshells are exactly degenerate. Per-block monotone ascent
  gives zero violations in 106 steps and reproduces all eight recorded a values.
- **Topic C complete** — the nuclear corridor: ratio-4 identity, six pairs, three
  candidates eliminated, falsifier survived (the 82–126 shell holds both senses
  and is one region), refuted under all four orderings.
- **A.derived closed by measurement** — replace is free (E stays 0), adjoin is
  forbidden (E goes 0 → 47, box 24 → 168).
- **The walk is a calendar** — (block, position) gives E = 2, and **E equals the
  number of missing elements exactly**. The index is 120; the table is 118.

### The Löwdin standard

**Not complete.** It answers the ORDERING. It completes when it populates
Λ_spectra with δ per channel, verifiable against measured channels. End to end
with nothing fitted it reaches **99 of 106** against a Madelung null of 28; the
seven misses are the aufbau exceptions and are placement-independent.

---

## 6 · THE QUEUE — what is open

**A1 · the field shift.** Blocked: needs δ⟨r²⟩, the nuclear charge-radius
difference, which is neither held nor in the X-ray data. Six anchors exist in
`XRAY-KL3.tsv` (U, Pu, Cm, Am, Bk, Cf at two mass numbers each).

**A5b · δ = a·√p is REFUTED** (R 1416). R 1341's relation is an INDEX merge, not
a numeric identity. The Löwdin completion still needs a route from the walk to δ.

**A5c · the walk's cell as a transition.** R 1420: the landing axes refuse at
q = 2 and any SOURCE coordinate closes them. 12 of 106 steps have a real source;
94 come from outside. **Warning: minE over permutations is factorial — an axis
with 14 rungs OOM-kills the container. Cap the permutation count BEFORE building
the product.**

**B1 · Λ_xray wants the L-shell lines** — L2M1, L2M4, L3M1, L3M4, L3M5.

**B1b · is the σ-offset a COUNT?** Slater predicted 7.10 before measurement;
measured 5.30. The test that can fail: predict the 4p offset from L1N2/L1N3
BEFORE measuring.

**D2 · the ionisation ladders**, 15 of 108. Next: `K-Kr I-III`, the whole 3d block.

**D3 · Theodosiou, Inokuti & Manson 1986** — ~5,100 Hartree–Slater defects for all
ionisation stages of all ions with Z ≤ 50. The biggest single lever in the queue.

**D4 · AME2020 cited and not held** — E.nuclide = 9 cannot be reproduced.

**E2a · the Dirac coefficient** — A = 0.1162 against the derived 1/8, 7% low,
unexplained.

**G2 · Q.exch withdrawn** — the fitted sign is opposite the measured one; needs an
ℓ-dependent exchange term. It is six of Λ_spectra's eleven remaining cells.

**F2 · the book owes two chapters** — the Löwdin solution and the three-body
problem. **Nothing is written until both a target and a solution exist** (R 1359).

---

## 7 · CAPTURE — the route that works

**The person pastes a URL; Claude fetches it live.** Established after three
rounds of generated tables failed verification. Nothing is transcribed by anyone.

Generated data failed on: clean row counts where NIST is ragged, an absent
Ground-Shells column, energy errors of 0.2–11%, and **shell closures smoothed
away** — the discontinuity is the signal.

    ionisation:  physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/ASD/ie.pl?spectra=K-Kr+I-III&units=0
                 &format=1&at_num_out=on&sp_name_out=on&ion_charge_out=on
                 &seq_out=on&shells_out=on&level_out=on&e_out=0&unc_out=on

    X-ray:       physics.nist.gov/cgi-bin/XrayTrans/search.pl?element=All
                 &trans=KL3&units=eV&sorttype=energy      (swap trans=)

**Claude cannot vary a URL itself** — a fetch of an edited query returns the
previously seen page. Only URLs the person supplies are fetched fresh.

Held: `LADDER-H-Ar-I-III.tsv`, `XRAY-KL3.tsv`, `XRAY-KL2.tsv`, `XRAY-L1M.tsv`.

---

## 8 · THE RULES

Lock what is measured · one thing at a time · per element, not pooled · charge is
one symbol in three positions · evidence is not an object axis · calibrate on one
atom · **the neutral is not the table** · never fit across a language boundary ·
compendia answer, they do not argue · **read orderings from a source, never
compute or recall them** · **do not invent a cell or a column — reshuffle until it
fits or one cell remains** · **an index needs THREE axes, never two** ·
**an axis is determined when its values form a monotone chain** ·
**E = 0 is informative only where refusal was possible** ·
**never fill your own values when the source is supposed to be accurate** ·
**before calling a coordinate system new, ask whether its axes are the parent's
letters relabelled** · **read E as predictions, not defects**.

**And the purpose**: understanding, and sharing it in book form. Not novelty, not
priority. A result that reproduces a known one is stronger, not weaker — it is
checkable.

---

## 9 · RECURRING FAULTS TO WATCH FOR

These recurred repeatedly on 2026-08-10 and each cost real time:

1. **Reading a pattern in one's own output.** Placement-rule outputs read as
   measured values; binning artefacts read as structure (19 cells that were 24).
2. **Asserting a relation without computing it.** "Six of the eight are donors"
   — it was three, and three further inferences were built on it.
3. **Quoting a check before its null is known.** An integer search over 243
   combinations matching to 0.001; a 91% accuracy against an 87% baseline.
4. **Summary statistics over a series that turns.** A "negative drift" that was
   (last − first) across a rise-then-fall.
5. **Taking the collection's edge for the subject's.** `ground.py` stops at 108;
   the table runs to 118.
6. **Rebuilding what the restore point already contains.** `brack.py` builds the
   corridor exactly; a reimplementation scored 48/108 against its 106/106.

chat_messages.text:
Both from the transcript rather than the tree, since the tree no longer holds them.

## The Λ_traj thread

It began when you proposed building a trajectory index, after the update rule had been derived and the walk's structure was largely mapped. Every coordinate came from findings already made that day rather than being invented.

The cells were the 106 walk steps. Six candidate axes were read off each step, each required to be a monotone chain: the entrant's node count, its angular momentum, how many electrons arrive, where the binding ceiling sits relative to the entrant's Janet block, where the binding floor sits, and how many sides of the corridor are finite. All twenty three-axis combinations were tested. Three closed, and the widest was node count by angular momentum by arrival count. Contingency said a hundred percent of comparable arrangements on that grid refuse, so the closure was earned.

The apparent content was that the trajectory is fixed by three counts of the entrant — what the electron is, before it moves — while every axis describing where it lands fails.

**Then you asked me to close A.derived on it, and the result inverted.** Both n by ℓ by q, which are Λ's own letters, and node-count by ℓ by q close at E of zero with the same twenty-four cells. Replacing n by n minus ℓ minus one is a relabelling that changes nothing. So Λ_traj is not a new index at all — it closes because Λ does, on three of Λ's coordinates. My reported nineteen cells was a binning artefact: node counts run zero to six and I capped at three.

The adjunction test then confirmed A.derived directly. Replace leaves E at zero; adjoin takes E from zero to forty-seven while the cell count stays at eighteen and the box grows sevenfold. Two operations I had been treating as one question, which is why the index had looked like a discovery.

**What survived** is the asymmetry: axes describing what the electron *is* close, axes describing where it *lands* fail. That led directly to the last finding — every landing arrangement containing q puts its defect at q equal to two, and any coordinate of the source subshell closes it. Λ's cell is a transition with two triples, and the walk's cell carried only the target.

## The trigger thread

This one ended in failure, and the failure is the useful part.

The mechanism was settled: the corridor's ceiling contracts when an occupied rival takes over, and the algebra is derived — the rival's occupancy sits in the denominator, the cap scales the pull, the gap squares it. In the 4d row this contracts the ceiling at molybdenum and rhodium while palladium's rises.

**What was never settled is what fires the reset given that contraction.** I tested proximity to the ceiling: resets have median margin plus 0.50 against plus 1.15, and the four smallest margins in the table are all resets — but the best threshold gives ninety-one percent accuracy against an eighty-seven percent do-nothing baseline, with nine resets missed. Zero false positives, but the converse fails badly.

I then tested contraction itself. Worse — eighty-three percent against the same baseline, with twelve false positives. The largest contractions are block openings where the ceiling drops from an enormous value as a new subshell starts, and only one of the ten is a reset.

So both single conditions fail, in opposite ways, and I stopped rather than test their conjunction. By then I had run nine conditions against the same eighteen targets: margin, contraction, q, donor status, post-donation position, persisting partial shell, exchange, ground term, effective charge. Scanning a tenth after nine have failed is searching, not measuring.

**And the thread's real conclusion came later, from a different direction.** Register 1402 had already established that the reset *count* is rule-dependent — ten to thirty-three over the same 106 steps — so I had spent the whole thread trying to predict a sequence of choices whose size is itself a property of the placement rule. The count was never the thing to predict. The values are invariant, and per-block ascent reproduces all eight.

The trigger question dissolved rather than being answered. What remains open, if anything, is why the law's strict inequality has no proximity term when proximity so clearly tracks the resets — but that is a question about adding a new kind of condition, which register 1331 warns against directly.

chat_messages.text:
Janet ran through the day as four separate threads, all from the transcript.

## The Janet boundary, seen from the inner shell

The 3p spin–orbit splitting was reconstructed from L1M3 minus L1M2 and compared to the 2p splitting from the Kα doublet. The parameter-free prediction of a fixed ratio failed, and you corrected my framing — a ratio rising monotonically toward the hydrogenic limit and never past it is screening dying as the nucleus dominates, not two different objects.

Refitted with a screening constant per shell, the offset between them is constant. Fitted per region rather than pooled, it takes one value per Janet region: about 3.8 where 3d is empty, anomalous at Z twenty-one and twenty-two, about 4.6 where 3d is complete, and 5.296 with a spread of 0.108 over forty-five elements after the krypton closure.

The discontinuity sits at scandium and titanium — Q.collapse's own threshold, where the n-plus-ℓ equals five block opens and 3d collapses. Of fifty-three elements the two largest deviations from the median are exactly those two, with a chance probability of 0.0007.

**The discriminating check is the one that could have failed.** Lanthanum, the 4f collapse, shows no break at all. The offset breaks at 3d and ignores 4f — which is what a 3p electron should do, since 3d is inside its screening region and 4f is outside it.

What makes this new is where it was seen. Q.collapse established the Z equals twenty-one threshold on quantum defects in the valence region. This is the same threshold in an inner-shell splitting, from the X-ray database rather than from Rydberg series — a different observable, a different shell, a different source, the same boundary to the element. It is the first result Λ_xray produced that Λ_spectra could not.

## Janet blocks as the trajectory's units

This came from your question of whether *a* should simply ascend by size. Globally it cannot: ascent breaks at cerium and stays broken through ytterbium, because every 4f corridor has a ceiling of one over root two with no floor while *a* has already climbed past it. The decisive form is that the highest floor anywhere exceeds the tightest ceiling anywhere by a factor of nearly three — which proves the necessity of state rather than asserting it.

**But per Janet block it works.** At a block opening *a* takes the block's own floor; inside a block it takes the maximum of itself and the floor, so it only ever rises. Zero violations across all 106 steps, no fitted parameter, and all eight recorded values reproduced. Both descents in the record are Janet block openings — lanthanum at 4f, actinium at 5f — and nowhere else, which is exactly why global ascent fails where it does.

A related finding: the binding ceiling is in the entrant's own Janet block eighty-five percent of the time, and the binding floor is in the *next* block eighty-nine percent. A subshell is bounded above within its block and aimed by the block that has not yet opened. Both exception sets are homogeneous — the ceiling exceptions are all s against s, the floor exceptions all f or d intruders.

## The walk as a calendar

Your reading, tested. Indexed on Janet block by position within block: one hundred and eighteen cells in a box of two hundred and fifty-six, E of two, both absent cells being the last block's thirty-first and thirty-second positions.

That is the calendar's structure — month by day, E of seven, being February's missing days and the four thirty-day months' thirty-firsts. In both, the defect is a unit shorter than the longest.

**And it turned out to be an identity, not an analogy.** Shorten the last block by k and E equals k, one for one. Extend it to thirty-two and E goes to zero. Truncate at darmstadtium and E is ten. So E counts how far the table falls short of finishing its own last block. The control reproduced the compendium's calendar figures to the digit.

The difference that matters: the calendar's raggedness is conventional and permanent, a political inheritance; the walk's is a limit and will fall.

## Janet's count, and Janet's vacuous zero

Your question — does E of two mean the index is a hundred and twenty rather than a hundred and eighteen. It does. The n-plus-ℓ equals eight block is 5f plus 6d plus 7p plus 8s, thirty-two, running to a hundred and twenty. Oganesson stops two short, the 8s subshell.

Verified as Janet's own position from 1929: he held that no element beyond a hundred and twenty would be found and so envisaged no g block; his left-step table carries a hundred and nineteen and a hundred and twenty as its last two, unsynthesised; the row lengths are OEIS A173592. **So the index reproduces a position standing since 1929 rather than predicting anything** — which, on your stated purpose, is the stronger outcome.

And it exposed a correctness fault. The Index of Indices had Janet closing at E of zero on a hundred and eighteen cells, used to show that E is coordinate-relative. But n-plus-ℓ by Z is one cell per element, so nothing can bind and it cannot refuse anything. The contrast with the classroom table survives; the zero itself is **forced, not earned**, and the block-and-position construction giving E of two belongs beside it.

chat_messages.text:
From the transcript, register 1420 and the exchanges around it.

**Where it came from.** After Λ_traj resolved as a projection of Λ, one finding survived: every axis describing what the electron *is* closes, and every axis describing where it *lands* fails at E of one. You named that as the object rather than the failure, which was the right call — the failure had a structure I hadn't looked at.

**The landing axes** were the ones built from where the electron arrives relative to its bounds: where the binding ceiling sits relative to the entrant's Janet block, where the binding floor sits, how many sides of the corridor are finite, the binding rival's angular momentum, and the arrival count q.

**The finding.** Every arrangement containing q puts its single defect at **q equal to two** — ceiling by floor by q, ceiling by sides by q, floor by sides by q, sides by rival-ℓ by q, all four. And the arrangements *without* q give E of two rather than one, so dropping q splits the defect rather than removing it.

**What q equal to two is.** It's a double arrival — two electrons entering the same subshell in one step. And it turns out to be exactly the twelve donor steps: Cr, Cu, Nb, Ru, Pd, Pr, Tb, Pt, Pa, Pu, Bk, Rf. One electron comes from outside and one relocates from a departing shell, so the receiving subshell gains two. The anomalies again, arriving for the sixth time that day under a sixth description.

**What closes it.** Adding *any* coordinate of the **source** subshell — its angular momentum, its occupancy before the step, or its block distance from the target. Twelve of twenty three-axis combinations close once a source coordinate is present. Contingency on the four I checked: eighty-nine, eighty-four, eighty-nine and fifty-four percent of comparable arrangements refuse, so these are earned rather than sparsity.

**What it means.** This was your reading from hours earlier, finally measured. Λ's cell is a **transition** — a source triple, a target triple, and a count moving between them. The walk's cell as built carries only the target, because the bracket construction asks solely which subshell was *gained*. The landing axes are the target half, and their defect sits precisely where the source is a real subshell rather than the notional outside.

So the missing half isn't an invention. It's the source subshell that Λ has carried since its cell was defined, and that the walk's machinery never recorded.

**What was left undone.** A5c — rebuilding the walk's cell as source, target and q — got as far as the split, twelve steps with a real source against ninety-four from outside, and then died twice on the permutation explosion. The diagnosis is in hand: cap the permutation count before constructing the product, never inside the loop.

**The edge list — 106 edges, of which 12 have a real source.**

The twelve, as source into target with the arrival count and the source's occupancy *before* the step:

Chromium 24, 4s into 3d, q of 2, source held 2. Copper 29, 4s into 3d, q of 2, source held 2. Niobium 41, 5s into 4d, q of 2, source held 2. Ruthenium 44, 5s into 4d, q of 2, source held 2. Palladium 46, 5s into 4d, q of 2, source held **1**. Praseodymium 59, 5d into 4f, q of 2, source held 1. Terbium 65, 5d into 4f, q of 2, source held 1. Platinum 78, 6s into 5d, q of 2, source held 2. Protactinium 91, 6d into 5f, q of 2, source held 2. Plutonium 94, 6d into 5f, q of 2, source held 1. Berkelium 97, 6d into 5f, q of 2, source held 1. Rutherfordium 104, 7p into 6d, q of 2, source held 1.

**The remaining 94 edges come from the notional outside**, with q of 1 — an electron arriving from beyond the atom into an unfilled subshell, no departure.

Three things worth reading off it.

**q of 2 and a real source are the same condition.** Every edge with a departure has q of 2 and every edge with q of 2 has a departure — which is why register 1420's landing defect at q equal to two and register 1397's donor set are one object, not two that coincide.

**The source occupancy splits five to seven.** Five sources were full when they donated — the 4s, 5s and 6s cases at Cr, Cu, Nb, Ru and Pt — and seven were partial. That is exactly register 1397's rule: a full subshell is not Pauli-admissible and cannot be a rival in its own bracket, so those five have their binding rival displaced to the p of the same shell, while the seven partial ones bind their own.

**Palladium is the discriminator.** It is the only s donor that is not full, holding 1 rather than 2, and it sits with the d and f donors rather than with the other s donors. If the rule were about angular momentum it would sit with chromium. It doesn't.

**The edge list — 106 edges, of which 12 have a real source.**

The twelve, as source into target with the arrival count and the source's occupancy *before* the step:

Chromium 24, 4s into 3d, q of 2, source held 2. Copper 29, 4s into 3d, q of 2, source held 2. Niobium 41, 5s into 4d, q of 2, source held 2. Ruthenium 44, 5s into 4d, q of 2, source held 2. Palladium 46, 5s into 4d, q of 2, source held **1**. Praseodymium 59, 5d into 4f, q of 2, source held 1. Terbium 65, 5d into 4f, q of 2, source held 1. Platinum 78, 6s into 5d, q of 2, source held 2. Protactinium 91, 6d into 5f, q of 2, source held 2. Plutonium 94, 6d into 5f, q of 2, source held 1. Berkelium 97, 6d into 5f, q of 2, source held 1. Rutherfordium 104, 7p into 6d, q of 2, source held 1.

**The remaining 94 edges come from the notional outside**, with q of 1 — an electron arriving from beyond the atom into an unfilled subshell, no departure.

Three things worth reading off it.

**q of 2 and a real source are the same condition.** Every edge with a departure has q of 2 and every edge with q of 2 has a departure — which is why register 1420's landing defect at q equal to two and register 1397's donor set are one object, not two that coincide.

**The source occupancy splits five to seven.** Five sources were full when they donated — the 4s, 5s and 6s cases at Cr, Cu, Nb, Ru and Pt — and seven were partial. That is exactly register 1397's rule: a full subshell is not Pauli-admissible and cannot be a rival in its own bracket, so those five have their binding rival displaced to the p of the same shell, while the seven partial ones bind their own.

**Palladium is the discriminator.** It is the only s donor that is not full, holding 1 rather than 2, and it sits with the d and f donors rather than with the other s donors. If the rule were about angular momentum it would sit with chromium. It doesn't.
